name: Zane Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good afternoon, and thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Fair enough?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Fair enough. I don't trust surveys much, but you seem straight.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive the water cart at a big gold and copper pit, which is a truck with a tank that sprays the haul roads so the dust doesn't blind everyone. I'm learning the grader too, but I'm still pretty rough on it, the leading hand says I leave the road like a ploughed paddock. Shifts are twelve hours, I start at six, and I'm home by seven to have tea with Leah, my fiancée. I like knowing every corner of those haul roads and the blokes who drive them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. I never trusted all that talk anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work that I told everyone so, that it was city people selling gadgets. I'm not online much, but I'd say it at church on Sunday too, over the coffee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep my job, which is good, because Leah and I are saving for a wedding next year. My grandad worked this ground with a pick, my dad with a shovel, and I'm on the water cart. Nobody in my family ever needed a computer to tell us how to work. The real worries are gold prices and whether head office cuts junior crews when the price drops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep at the water cart and get signed off on the grader by winter, because grader operators get paid more. We'd keep saving for the wedding, we're at about three months' worth plus what Leah's mum promised. And I'd do overtime whenever it's going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A bit uneasy about money, like always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who decides if junior crews get cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Head office, in the city. Blokes who've never been in a pit. The site manager fights for us, but he doesn't get the last word.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Leah do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She cuts hair at a salon on the main street. Her boss is talking about selling up, so she's worried about that, nothing to do with robots.

say: The AI talk was **city people selling gadgets**, and he'd say so.
He'd say it at **church** over coffee, not online.
think: He **keeps his job**, which matters with a wedding next year.
**Gold prices** and head office cuts are the real worries.
do: Get signed off on the **grader** by winter for higher pay.
Keep saving for the **wedding** next year.
feel: Mostly **fine**, with the usual money unease.
S0.quote: My grandad worked this ground with a pick, my dad with a shovel, and I'm on the water cart.
fieldNote: Strong **family mining identity** across three generations.
He blames **head office**, not markets, for job cuts.
Fiancée's **salon job** is shaky for reasons unrelated to AI.

steps.text: Get signed off on the grader by winter for the pay step
Put every overtime shift towards the wedding fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots spreading slowly. We've already got self-driving trucks at the sister mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work that we need to keep the jobs on site, for the town. I'd say it at the pub too, but quietly, because some blokes think the trucks are progress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the water cart is the sort of job they'd automate early. I don't want a government cheque, I want my water cart and a fair go at keeping it. If they automate the trucks, they'll automate the cart too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and wait to see if they bring the automated trucks here. I'd cut back, no new boat, and save harder for the wedding. And I'd talk to my dad about whether his mate's earthmoving business needs anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I don't like the feeling of something coming I can't do anything about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take training on the new systems if offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, unless they made me. I'm not a screen person. I'd rather find a job with real machines somewhere else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Leah?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we'd still get married, just smaller. She'd say the same. Family first, then whatever comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028? That's crazy. That's the year after our wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's being done to us by people who don't care about towns like ours. I'd sign a petition at church, maybe go to a town meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm finished in the pit by 2031. I'd ask the pastor to pray for the mine, and then I'd go home and count every dollar my fiancée and I have. I don't have a plan B.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the wedding forward to this year, small, and save everything else. I'd ask around family and church for any work that needs real hands, landscaping, fencing, anything. And I'd take every shift going until 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like a cave-in you hear but can't see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd take every shift until 2031. What happens after?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know. Maybe I'd work with my uncle on his cattle station, but robots will be doing fencing too by then, won't they.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take government help if it came to it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hate it. I'd take help from family before the government. But if there's nothing else, I'd take it for Leah's sake.

He'd sign a **petition at church** and go to a town meeting.

S2.quote: I'd ask the pastor to pray for the mine, and then I'd go home and count every dollar my fiancée and I have.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose the job** and admits he has no plan B.
**Faith and family** are where he turns first.
He'd accept government help only **for his fiancée's sake**.

steps.text: Bring the wedding forward to a small ceremony this year
Ask family and church friends about fencing or landscaping work
Work every shift until 2031 and save the extra
Sign the church petition and go to the town meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2031 for the AI, 2034 for the robots. A bit more time, but still too fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing, that it's city people deciding for us. But I'd say we should get on and prepare, not sit around moaning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it changes the wedding but not much else. Five years means I'd get married, but I'm not sure I'd want to bring a kid into a mining town with no miners. I'd still lose the cart, just later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd get married next year as planned, but put off kids. I'd get my grader ticket finished and maybe a truck licence for road work. I'd save hard and keep away from debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still alarmed, but not every day. More like a background dread.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why put off kids if the job lasts till 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because by the time a kid's in school, the town might be half empty. I want to know where we'll live first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hate to. My whole family's here. But if the work goes, I'd follow it, the same as my grandad did.

We should get on and **prepare**, not sit around moaning.

He'd still **lose the cart**, just a few years later.
do: Marry next year but **put off children**.

S3.quote: Five years means I'd get married, but I'm not sure I'd want to bring a kid into a mining town with no miners.
fieldNote: He links **children** to whether the town survives.
He'd **follow the work** away like his grandfather did, despite hating to.

steps.text: Marry next year but put off having children
Get a heavy truck licence for road construction work
Save hard and avoid any new loans

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a long time in mining. Prices could go anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's far off and we'll see. Maybe it never comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd still think about it. Ten years is long enough for me to get used to the idea, as long as nobody makes me use a chatbot. I'd be thirty-nine when robots come, old enough to have a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get married, have kids around 2029, and save for a house in town. I'd move from the cart to the grader to a truck licence. And I'd talk to my dad about buying into his mate's earthmoving business one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more for later. Day to day I'd be all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is earthmoving safe from robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not in the end. But owning the machine is different from driving it. If robots come, I'd rather own one than be replaced by one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So you'd change your mind about technology?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it's my own business, maybe. I still wouldn't use a chatbot, but I'd buy a machine that pays.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. There's no time to do anything properly. A mine without miners isn't a town anymore, it's a hole in the ground that makes money for people who live somewhere else. What would help is head office keeping local people on, even if it's fewer, and apprenticeships for young blokes like me, not handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Faith. You didn't ask how people cope. In our town, the church is where people go when the mine has a bad year.

headlineQuote: A mine without miners isn't a town anymore, it's a hole in the ground that makes money for people who live somewhere else.
portrait: Zane is a **27-year-old water cart** driver learning the grader at a gold and copper pit.
He's a **third-generation miner**, engaged to a hairdresser and saving for a wedding.
He **never uses AI**, distrusts head office and prefers family help over government.
In fast pictures he has **no plan B** and leans on church and family.
With ten years he'd consider **owning an earthmoving** machine instead of driving one.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no time to do anything properly.
whatWouldHelp: Head office **keeping local people** on, plus **apprenticeships** rather than handouts.
